guide.summary: Unit 4 introduces Vergil's Aeneid through Books 1 and 2: the epic's purpose and proem, Juno's anger and the storm, Jupiter's prophecy of Roman destiny, the Trojans' arrival in Carthage, and Aeneas' account of Troy's fall.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Vergil (70–19 BCE) wrote the Aeneid under Augustus, after decades of civil war, connecting Rome's origins to the Trojan hero Aeneas, ancestor of the Julian family. The poem imitates and transforms Homer: Books 1–6 resemble the Odyssey (wandering), Books 7–12 the Iliad (war). Its central virtue is pietas, duty to gods, family, and country, often at personal cost. The meter is dactylic hexameter.

sections.heading: Book 1
sections.body: The proem (1.1–7) announces the theme: arms and the man who, exiled by fate, came from Troy to Italy, tossed on land and sea by the power of the gods because of Juno's unforgetting anger, and suffered in war until he could found a city and bring his gods to Latium, the origin of the Latin race, the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome. Juno hates the Trojans because of the judgment of Paris, her love for Carthage, and Ganymede; she bribes Aeolus to unleash a storm. Aeneas, in despair, wishes he had died at Troy ('O terque quaterque beati'). Neptune calms the sea, compared in the poem's first simile to a respected statesman calming a rioting crowd. Venus complains to Jupiter, who reveals Rome's destiny and promises 'imperium sine fine'. In Carthage, Aeneas sees scenes of the Trojan War on Juno's temple and weeps ('sunt lacrimae rerum'). Dido, a refugee queen founding a new city, welcomes the Trojans.

sections.heading: Book 2
sections.body: At Dido's banquet, Aeneas narrates Troy's fall. The Trojans find the wooden horse; Laocoön warns them not to trust it ('timeo Danaos et dona ferentes') and hurls a spear into it. The Greek Sinon, posing as a deserter, tells a deceptive story, and two serpents from the sea kill Laocoön and his sons, convincing the Trojans to bring the horse inside. That night, Hector's ghost tells Aeneas to flee with Troy's gods. Aeneas fights in fury, witnesses Pyrrhus kill Priam at the altar, and is restrained by Venus, who shows him the gods destroying Troy. After a divine sign (a flame on Iulus' head), Aeneas carries his father Anchises on his shoulders and leads Iulus by the hand, with his wife Creusa following; Creusa is lost, and her ghost foretells his future in Italy. The image of Aeneas carrying his father became the emblem of pietas.

sections.heading: Themes to track
sections.body: Several themes run through Books 1 and 2. Fate (fatum) drives Aeneas toward Italy despite suffering. Pietas defines him as dutiful to gods, family, and people. Divine anger, especially Juno's, causes much of the suffering, while Venus protects her son. Loss and memory appear in Aeneas's grief for Troy and his reaction to the temple images in Carthage. Leadership is tested as Aeneas hides his own despair to encourage his men, saying that one day it may be pleasing to remember even these things.

sections.heading: Vergil's style
sections.body: Vergil uses similes to connect events to broader human experience, such as the statesman calming a crowd or the bees building Carthage. He uses enjambment to create suspense, alliteration and assonance for sound effects, and spondaic lines to slow the rhythm in solemn moments. Speeches reveal character: Laocoön's warning, Sinon's deceptive story, and Hector's ghost each show rhetorical skill. Questions often ask you to identify a device and explain its effect in context.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: Know the context of every syllabus passage: who is speaking, to whom, where in the story, and what happens just before and after.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: Aeneas's character develops across Books 1 and 2. In the storm he despairs, wishing he had died at Troy, but he hides his fear to encourage his men. In Book 2, he first rushes into battle in fury, seeking a glorious death, before divine signs and his family redirect him to his duty: carrying his father, leading his son, and preserving Troy's gods. This shift from personal heroism to pietas toward family and future is central to the poem and often appears in essay questions about leadership and duty.

keyTakeaways: Proem: arma virumque, fato profugus, Juno's anger, founding Rome.
Juno's grievances; the storm; first simile.
commonMistakes: Confusing Laocoön's warning with Sinon's lie.
Calling Aeneas a typical Homeric hero; he is defined by pietas.
Mixing up Book 1 (storm, Carthage) and Book 2 (Troy's fall).
examTips: Memorize the proem and translate it literally.
Know who speaks each famous line.

rubric.description: Arma virumque cano → I sing of arms and the man
Troiae qui primus ab oris → who first from the shores of Troy
Italiam ... Laviniaque venit litora → came to Italy and the Lavinian shores
multum ille ... iactatus → he (was) much tossed
et terris et alto → both on lands and on the deep
vi superum → by the force of the gods above
saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram → because of the unforgetting anger of cruel Juno
multa quoque et bello passus → having suffered many things also in war
dum conderet urbem → until he could found a city
inferretque deos Latio → and bring (his) gods into Latium
genus unde Latinum → from where (came) the Latin race
Albanique patres → and the Alban fathers
moenia Romae → the walls of Rome

practice.sampleResponse: I sing of arms and the man who first from the shores of Troy came, exiled by fate, to Italy and the Lavinian shores; he was much tossed both on lands and on the deep by the force of the gods above, because of the unforgetting anger of cruel Juno; having suffered many things also in war, until he could found a city and bring his gods into Latium, from where came the Latin race, and the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
